passage: At the Class 10 assembly in a Mumbai school, the vice principal announced a new rule: no talking in the library at any time, including the project room. Sabina raised her hand. "Ma'am, who decided this, and what is it for? Group projects need talking." A murmur ran along the row. "Rules are rules, Sabina." Jyoti shrank in her seat and pulled at Sabina's sleeve; Rahul gave a thumbs-up under his desk. Sabina stayed standing. "I am not saying we should break it. I want to know why." The vice principal paused. "Meet me at lunch." Sabina's knees shook as she sat down.

qa.q: What new rule did the vice principal announce?
qa.a: The vice principal announced no talking in the library at any time, including the project room.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when pulling at Sabina's sleeve?
qa.a: Jyoti was anxious, fearing trouble for Sabina and perhaps for the row; the tug shows a wish for Sabina to sit down.

qa.q: What choice by Sabina kept the question respectful?
qa.a: Sabina said she was not saying to break the rule and only wanted to know why, which separated testing a rule from defiance.

qa.q: How might the vice principal see Sabina's question?
qa.a: The vice principal may first read it as defiance, given "Rules are rules", but the pause and the invitation to meet at lunch suggest some openness.

grounding: A teenager begins asking why a rule exists and who made it, which looks like defiance to adults expecting quick compliance.

passage: "Phones go off at ten," said Papa, tapping the table. "Why ten, Papa? Who decided?" asked Aparna. "I did." "But why not eleven? Riya's parents say eleven." "Aparna, do not compare." "I am not being rude. I just want to know the reason." Mummy looked up from her plate, and little Ronit, with his spoon halfway to his mouth, went very still. Papa sighed. "Sleep. School." "Then can I show you my timetable on Sunday and we decide together?" Papa was quiet. "Anirban, let her show you," said Mummy. Papa nodded slowly. "Show me on Sunday."

qa.q: What time did Papa say the phones go off?
qa.a: Papa said the phones go off at ten.

qa.q: How does Aparna feel about the ten o'clock rule, and what shows it?
qa.a: Aparna feels curious and a little frustrated, pressing “why ten” and “who decided” because she wants the reason, not to be rude.

qa.q: What choice did Aparna make that turned the argument into a talk?
qa.a: Aparna offered to show her timetable on Sunday and decide together, which gave Papa a way to say yes without losing authority.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ronit at the table while Aparna and Papa argue?
qa.a: Ronit went very still, which suggests tension and worry about the argument getting bigger.

grounding: A teenager asks why a rule exists and who made it, healthy testing that can look like defiance to a parent expecting quick compliance.

passage:
I'm Gurleen, and looking back at Class 10, I think that was the year I started asking why.
Our school rule said girls must wear two plaits with black ribbons. Boys had no hair rule at all. One morning in assembly line, Ms Shalini told me to redo my single plait. I asked, “Ma'am, who made this rule, and why only for girls?”
The line went dead silent. A few girls stared at their shoes. My friend Harleen whispered, “Are you mad?”
Ms Shalini said, “Don't argue, just do it.” My mother, later, called it attitude.
But I wasn't trying to be rude. I truly wanted to know. That week I read the school diary and found the rule was from 1987. Nobody I asked could explain it.

qa.q: What colour ribbons did the rule say girls must wear?
qa.a: Black ribbons.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel about being called rude?
qa.a: Gurleen felt misunderstood and frustrated, because the question came from real curiosity, not a wish to be rude.

qa.q: How could Gurleen raise the question in a way adults might hear better?
qa.a: Gurleen could ask for a quiet time with the teacher or write to the principal, sharing the rule's date and asking for its reason.

qa.q: How might Harleen have felt in that silent line?
qa.a: Harleen was probably nervous and a bit shocked, worried Gurleen would get into trouble, which is why Harleen whispered.

grounding: A teenager recalls starting to ask why a rule exists and who made it, which adults read as defiance though it was honest questioning.

passage:
Class 10-A, note to self and to the class teacher, Friday.
In today's civics period, Jeevan asked why phones must be locked away even during lunch break, and who decided this. His tone was sharp. Raghav and a few others laughed, and I felt the class watching to see what I would do.
My first thought was that this was cheek. I nearly sent him out. Instead I asked, “Good question. Do you know who made the rule?” He didn't. None of them did.
I have asked Jeevan to find out from the office and bring a short written proposal by next Friday. He looked surprised, then nodded. I'll check in with him on Monday.

qa.q: What did Jeevan ask about phones?
qa.a: He asked why phones must be locked away even during lunch break, and who decided this.

qa.q: What was Jeevan likely feeling when he asked the question sharply?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and curious, wanting a real reason, perhaps a little defiant with the class watching.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do instead of sending him out, and why was it wise?
qa.a: They took the question seriously and asked Jeevan to find out and write a proposal, turning a challenge into healthy thinking.

qa.q: How might Raghav and the others see the moment?
qa.a: They laughed, so they may have expected a clash, and were probably surprised to see the question treated as a good one.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager asking why a rule exists and who made it, sees it first as cheek, then treats it as healthy testing.

passage:
Sunday night
Big fight at Mausi's housewarming. I didn't mean it to be a fight.
The rule was: kids eat after all the men finish. I asked Bade Papa, just asked, “Who made this rule? Why can't we eat together?” Samir choked on his lassi. The aunties went silent. Bade Papa said, “Since when does Shankar question elders?”
Mummy pulled me into the kitchen and said I embarrassed her. But I wasn't being cheeky! I really want to know. If it's about respect, fine, then say that. If it's just habit, why keep it?
Samir said later, “Bro, I also think it's weird, but I'm not saying it.” So I'm the villain and he agrees with me. Great.

qa.q: What was the rule at the housewarming?
qa.a: The rule was that kids eat after all the men finish.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel after being pulled into the kitchen by Mummy?
qa.a: Shankar felt misunderstood and frustrated, having asked out of real curiosity, not to be cheeky.

qa.q: What might help Shankar ask about family customs next time?
qa.a: Shankar could ask one elder privately and calmly, at a quiet time, instead of in front of all the guests.

qa.q: How might Samir see the whole scene?
qa.a: Samir privately agrees with Shankar but stays silent, so he may feel both relieved and a little guilty for not speaking up.

grounding: A teenager asks why a family rule exists and who made it, and adults who expect quick compliance read it as defiance.

passage:
Class 10B chat, 9:40 pm
Payal: ok but WHO decided we can't use the side gate after 2 pm?? it's literally closer to the bus stop
Vandana: Payal pls don't start 😅 just use the main gate
Payal: I will. I just want to know why
Ishaan: guard uncle said it's the principal's order
Payal: fine but what's the reason? if it's safety, I get it. if it's just "because", that's different
Vandana: you sound like you're picking a fight
Payal: I'm asking a question, not jumping the wall
Payal: said this at dinner and got told I'm getting "too argumentative"
Ishaan: my dad says that every time I ask why curfew is 8
Vandana: ok but maybe ask in council, not in here
Payal: yeah. writing it now: "May we know the reason for the side-gate rule?" polite enough?
Vandana: polite enough 👍

qa.q: After what time can students not use the side gate?
qa.a: After 2 pm.

qa.q: How does Payal feel when Vandana says it sounds like picking a fight?
qa.a: Payal feels irritated and misunderstood, because to Payal it is a real question about the reason, not an attack on the rule.

qa.q: How does Payal turn the question into something adults may hear better?
qa.a: Payal plans to ask in council with a polite written line asking for the reason, instead of arguing in the chat.

qa.q: Why might Vandana react to the rule differently from Payal?
qa.a: Vandana seems nervous about getting into trouble, so questioning feels risky and quiet compliance feels safer 😅

grounding: Illustrates a teenager starting to ask why a rule exists and who made it, which adults and peers can mistake for defiance.
